## 2

I hear where you’re coming from regarding skepticism about institutional images, but we actually don't need satellite photos or modern space agencies to know the Earth is a curved sphere. People figured that out thousands of years ago using simple, repeatable observations anyone can verify.

For instance, during a lunar eclipse, the Earth casts a shadow on the Moon, and that shadow is always circular—something only a sphere can produce regardless of orientation. Or consider travel: if you fly south toward the equator and past it, constellations like the North Star disappear below the horizon, while entirely new constellations, like the Southern Cross, rise into view. That shift wouldn’t happen on a flat plane. Even the fact that ships disappear bottom-first over the horizon, or that time zones exist with the sun rising in Tokyo while it’s dark in New York, relies entirely on curvature. 

I’m always open to questioning assumptions, but the sheer weight of everyday geometry and physics points to a round Earth.

## 3

To understand why the sky is blue, we first have to look at sunlight. Even though sunlight looks white or yellowish to us, it’s actually a mix of every color in the rainbow, all traveling together in waves.

Each color travels in a different wave size. Red and orange have long, lazy wavelengths, while blue and violet have short, choppy ones.

When sunlight hits Earth’s atmosphere, it crashes into a sea of invisible gas molecules (mostly nitrogen and oxygen). The long waves, like red and yellow, mostly pass straight through without bumping into much. But the short, choppy blue waves smack right into those tiny gas molecules and bounce off in every possible direction. 

Scientists call this **Rayleigh scattering**. Because blue light gets scattered and bounced around across the entire atmosphere, whenever you look up away from the sun, your eyes are catching that scattered blue light coming from every angle. 

(And if you're wondering why the sky isn't violet—since violet light has even shorter waves—it's because the sun emits much more blue light than violet, and human eyes happen to be far more sensitive to blue.)
